title: Thinking hard
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino starts from a familiar frustration: a teacher explains, models, questions and sets practice, yet students sit passively and forget. Her answer is that the teacher has done nothing wrong, and that a simple three-step technique can help students think hard in the moment of teaching: focus and maintain attention, frame the new knowledge, and gather information on what meaning students have made. For attention she recommends a rehearsed routine with a distinct cue such as STAR, narrated positively, and planned pauses with mini-whiteboards or cold calling. Framing links new content to prior knowledge and the next step, and gathering information moves from simple questions to ones that test real understanding, using turn and talk before whiteboards. It is a practical, example-rich piece grounded in a chemistry lesson.
points: Effortful teaching does not guarantee students think hard, so teachers need a deliberate technique for the moment of instruction.
Attention comes first, and it is secured through a rehearsed routine with a distinct cue and positive narration.
Framing explicitly connects new knowledge to what students already know and where it leads.
Teachers must check what meaning students have made, building from simple questions to ones that probe understanding.
Turn and talk combined with mini-whiteboards gives students processing time and builds their confidence.
quotes: I know that when I am hungry (which is basically my constant state of existence) or tired, I struggle to concentrate. This doesn’t mean it is unattainable. We can get our students thinking hard for the majority of lessons.

If students are not listening to you, we cannot get them thinking hard. This has to be the first step. The best way to ensure students listen to you and know that they must listen to what are you are about to say is to make this a routine.

As with everything we do in the classroom, we need to give students every chance to succeed and that includes succeeding at following STAR. When counting down to STAR (or another cue you might use), narrate the actions you want to see.

Asking questions and expecting responses really quickly can seem like the perfect solution but not all students process information in the same way or at the same speed. A way I get round this is to plan when I will pause explanations, ask questions on mini-whiteboards and then continue with my explanation.
Students are attending to the new bit of knowledge. They have been told why this new bit of knowledge is impoartant. But what happens in the mind of the learner is up to them and not you.

Focus and maintain attention. Frame the new knowledge, providing context. Gather information to check understanding and to determine what meaning has been made. Do these to help students think hard about what they are learning in the classroom.
